jobResponsibilities:
Strategic Audit Leadership

You will direct the planning, management, and execution of risk-based audit engagements across agencies under AGD's portfolio of clients, ensuring timely delivery and consistently high audit quality. Moving beyond traditional compliance-focused auditing, you will develop and maintain a forward-looking audit universe that reflects emerging risks and align audit priorities with the broader governance and risk landscape of the public sector. You will also champion agile auditing methodologies, designing shorter and more iterative audit cycles that deliver faster, more actionable insights to stakeholders.

Digital Transformation 

You will lead the integration of data analytics, robotic process automation (RPA), and AI-assisted audit tools into the audit methodology to enable continuous monitoring and deeper audit insights. You will oversee the adoption of audit management platforms to improve workflow efficiency and documentation standards. Staying ahead of developments in generative AI, machine learning, and other emerging technologies, you will assess their applicability to the IA function and build the team's capacity to leverage these tools effectively. Experience with data analytics tools such as Power BI, or Python in an audit context will be particularly valued.

Emerging Risk and Advisory

As a strategic advisor, you will engage credibly with C-suite and senior public sector leadership, translating complex audit findings into clear, business-relevant insights that drive meaningful governance improvements. You will provide assurance and advisory perspectives on a broadened risk landscape, including IT general controls, cybersecurity risk, digital business processes, third-party and supply chain risk, and increasingly, sustainability and ESG governance frameworks. You will work closely with agency leadership to anticipate risks before they materialise, positioning IA as a forward-looking function rather than a retrospective one.

Community Building and Capability Development

You will work with IA heads across the public sector to build a vibrant community of practice, driving the development of shared frameworks, toolkits, and upskilling programmes that raise the overall standard of public sector IA. You will implement capability development roadmaps that equip IA practitioners with both technical audit competencies and digital skills — including data literacy, AI fluency, and agile ways of working. You will represent AGD in cross-agency forums and professional bodies to advance the ambition of public sector IA.

People Leadership and Culture

You will manage, mentor, and develop a team of IA professionals, building a pipeline of future audit leaders who are technically strong, digitally capable, and strategically minded. You will foster a team culture that values psychological safety, diversity of thought, intellectual curiosity, and a genuine commitment to public service excellence. Attracting and retaining talent in a competitive market will be an important part of your mandate.

•	You should have demonstrated experience applying data analytics tools in an audit context, familiarity with AI-assisted audit platforms, and a working understanding of IT general controls, cybersecurity risk, and ESG governance. The Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) is a uniformed organisation under the purview of the Ministry of Home Affairs. The main role of SCDF is to provide fire-fighting, rescue and emergency ambulance services; mitigating hazardous materials incidents, as well as formulate, implement and enforce regulations on fire safety and civil defence shelter matters.

In 1982, the National Civil Defence Plan was launched which spearheaded the emergency preparedness for the nation. With the enactment of the Civil Defence Act in 1986, the SCDF was established as an independent organisation under the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA). In the same year, the Hotel New World collapse paved the way for joint operations between the SCDF and Singapore Fire Service (SFS). Due to the similarity in roles and functions, the SCDF and SFS were formally integrated on 15 April 1989.

Over the years, the SCDF has improved its life saving operations through innovations and programmes to enhance her fire-fighting, rescue capabilities and public education plans. The Light Fire Attack Vehicle (The Red Rhino) and Tracked Fire-Fighting Vehicle are some of the customized solutions which the force has developed to increase its operational capabilities. The SCDF also actively engages the local community through its wide-ranging public educational programmes and community-based activities to enhance the resilience and emergency preparedness of the civilian population.

Today, the Force is recognised by the population as a professional body of well-trained officers and men geared to respond to all types of life-threatening emergencies round-the-clock. An operationally ready SCDF, working hand-in-hand with a prepared and resilient population, helps to ensure that the nation is capable of handling any untoward eventualities.

jobDescription:
Looking for a job that actually makes a difference?
Join us at the Forefront of Shaping Healthier Lives

The Health Promotion Board’s vision is to make Singapore a nation of healthier people.
Come be a part of this journey if you’re passionate about creating boundary-pushing work that drives behavioral change.
You will be part of HPB’s Integrated Outreach team, which aims to create a Health Living Environment (HLE) where we make healthy living as part of every day life in Singapore. We aim to do so by place making, activating communities and empowering community leaders to play a role in health promotion. This transformative project shifts HPB's role from traditional programme provider to community enabler, embedding health promotion into citizens' lived environments across entire neighbourhoods. We are seeking a dynamic and strategic Manager/Senior Manager to spearhead community activation and drive sustainable behavioural change together with healthcare cluster (SingHealth, National University Hospital Systems, National Healthcare Group) and other community partners at the town level.
jobResponsibilities:
As a core member of the HLE initiative, you will be responsible for operationalising an innovative approach to community health that reaches the unreached and transforms neighbourhoods into health-promoting ecosystems. This role represents HPB's strategic pivot towards citizen-centric, place-based health interventions that integrate clinical care with lifestyle support anchored in local communities. You will develop skills in translating data insights into clear strategies and practical actions, data storytelling, stakeholder engagement and negotiation, project management, and cross-agency coordination.

Regional Roll out and Coordination of HLE

Programme Activation and Targeted Outreach

  • Coordinate community and regional health programmes, ensuring they are relevant to residents and responsive to their needs

  • Connect residents to healthy living assets and programmes by enlivening the lived environment and the Healthy 365 online-offline resident journey, through local mapping that guides them from discovery to sustained participation.

Monitoring, Feedback and Continuous Improvement

  • Track ground-level progress of HLE initiatives, consolidate feedback from residents, local stakeholders, and share insights with the project team and data teams to strengthen impact measurement

GovTech Data Practice


The Data Practice drives innovation and sets best practices for the effective and responsible use of data across the Whole-of-Government (WOG). AI is rapidly transforming how governments deliver services and how public officers work.

At GovTech's AI Programme, we build the platforms and experiences that enable Singapore's public service to safely and effectively adopt AI at scale. As a Designer, you will help shape the next generation of AI-powered experiences used across government. You'll work on products ranging from AI assistants that support thousands of public officers to developer platforms that enable teams to build trusted AI applications.

This is a hands-on product design role where you'll take ideas from discovery through delivery. You'll partner closely with other designers, product managers, engineers, and data scientists to uncover user needs, prototype solutions, validate assumptions, and ship experiences that are intuitive, trustworthy, and impactful.

We are looking for designers who don't just produce screens, but help shape product direction through research, experimentation, collaboration, and continuous iteration.

[What you will be working on]

You'll contribute across multiple AI initiatives, including:

  • AI-powered assistants — Designing conversational and task-oriented experiences that help public officers work more efficiently while maintaining trust, transparency, and appropriate human oversight.

  • AI Platforms — Improving the tools and workflows that enable government teams to build, evaluate, and deploy AI applications at scale.

  • Research across government — Understanding the diverse needs of ministries and agencies, translating complex workflows into simple, usable experiences.

  • Design systems and interaction patterns — Helping establish reusable patterns for AI interactions, ensuring consistency across products.

Key Responsibilities

User Research & Discovery

  • Plan and conduct discovery research to understand user needs, behaviours, and pain points faced by public officers across agencies.

  • Design and run usability testing sessions to validate concepts and iterate on designs.

  • Plan and facilitate surveys, workshops, and other participatory research methods to gather insights at scale.

  • Synthesise research findings into actionable insights and communicate them clearly to product and engineering teams.

UX & UI Design

  • Design end-to-end user experiences, covering information architecture, user flows, wireframes, and high-fidelity UI.

  • Design interactions that are intuitive, accessible, and aligned with both user needs and business objectives.

  • Build interactive prototypes in Figma to communicate design intent, making effective use of components and design system libraries.

  • Contribute to and maintain design systems, ensuring consistency across products.

  • Balance user needs, technical constraints, and policy requirements when making design decisions.

AI-Specific Design

  • Apply responsible AI design principles to surface model limitations, manage user expectations, and design for trust, transparency, and appropriate human oversight.

  • Work with product and engineering teams to design for AI-specific interaction patterns, including prompt interfaces, streaming responses, error and fallback states, and confidence indicators.

  • Advocate for ethical, inclusive, and human-centred approaches to AI product design.

Stakeholder Communication & Collaboration

  • Present design work and research findings to a range of stakeholders, including product managers, engineers, and senior government leaders.

  • Translate complex requirements and feedback into a clear design direction.

  • Communicate confidently with senior stakeholders and navigate differing perspectives constructively.

  • Work closely with product, data science and engineering teams to ensure designs are feasible and well-implemented.

What we are looking for

  • 3–5 years of experience designing digital products, supported by a strong portfolio that demonstrates user-centred thinking and excellent visual craftsmanship.

  • Experience taking products from discovery through delivery, partnering closely with cross-functional teams.

  • Strong research skills, with the ability to select appropriate methods, synthesize insights, and translate findings into product decisions.

  • Excellent interaction and visual design skills, with proficiency in Figma and modern design systems.

  • Strong communication and storytelling skills, with the confidence to present to both technical teams and senior stakeholders.

  • Curiosity about AI and emerging interaction patterns, with an interest in designing trustworthy human-AI experiences.

  • Ability to thrive in ambiguity, navigate complexity, and balance competing priorities.

  • Ability to think in systems, identifying reusable interaction patterns that scale across multiple AI products.

Nice to Have

  • Experience designing AI-powered products, conversational interfaces, or copilots.

  • Familiarity with prompt engineering, LLM evaluation, or AI product development workflows.

  • Experience working with design systems in complex product ecosystems.

  • Basic frontend development skills (HTML, CSS, React) to support rapid prototyping.

  • Experience with AI-assisted design and development tools such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude, or ChatGPT.

  • Motion design experience, including micro-interactions and animation using Lottie or After Effects.

  • Experience designing for government, enterprise SaaS, or highly regulated environments.

What it is like working here

We build products that serve a variety of agency users, who use them to solve highly meaningful problems pertinent to our society, from transportation, to education, to healthcare. We are here to improve how we live as a society through what we can offer as a government.

  • Rapid Prototyping - Instead of spending too much time debating ideas we prefer testing them. This identifies potential problems quickly, and more importantly, conveys what is possible to others easily.

  • Reliable Productisation - To scale an idea, a prototype or a Minimum Viable Product to a software product, we scrutinize and commit to its usability, reliability, scalability and maintainability.

  • Ownership - In addition to design responsibilities, this means having ideas on how things should be done and taking responsibility for seeing them through. Building something that you believe in is the best way to build something good.

  • Continuous Learning - Working on new ideas often means not fully understanding what you are working on. Taking time to learn new frameworks, technologies, and even different ways of working is not just encouraged but essential.

[What you will be working on]

Some problems are easy to walk past. Others keep nagging at you.
Why are we still doing this manually?
Why does sensible policy become painful when it meets the real world?
Why do we discover risks after the fact when the signals were already there?

How should government govern AI systems that increasingly make decisions and take actions for themselves? And why, when technology can change in minutes, does governance sometimes still move in months?

If questions like these bother you enough that you want to get underneath them, experiment with better answers and solve the real-world problem, we should talk.

We are rethinking what modern governance, risk and assurance could look like across GovTech and, ultimately, the wider Singapore Government.

GovTech is where we can design, build, test and learn. The ambition is bigger.

Why this matters

We are modernising Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) so government can use technology and AI with greater confidence, improve services faster, and keep the essential systems people rely on dependable and resilient.

Ultimately, the test is bigger than GRC: Can government use technology better, serve citizens better, and retain their trust when things go wrong?

That is the problem behind this role. And we do not expect to solve it by designing the perfect framework in a room.

We expect to work on real systems, with real users and real constraints. To experiment. Test assumptions. Prototype, understand behavior and incentives. Learn from what does not work.

And turn what does into something that can work at government scale. One role. Multiple archetypes. This is one modern GRC role, not six separate jobs or six career tracks.

The six archetypes below describe different capabilities a Modern GRC Practitioner can develop and create a problem.

You might begin with strength in one. Over time, you can acquire additional archetypes without giving up the ones you already have. An engineer might combine GRC Platform Engineering with Policy Engineering and AI Governance. An assurance practitioner might bring together Threat-Informed Risk Intelligence, Enterprise Risk Management and Systems Architecture. A policy practitioner might combine Policy Engineering with behavioral insights, systems thinking and platform capability.

Which archetypes you draw on depends on the problem. Some practitioners will build deep expertise in one or two. Others will develop a broader combination across several. Neither is a prescribed progression. The archetypes are not boxes to move between. They are capabilities you can accumulate, combine and apply. The ambition is to build practitioners with an increasingly powerful repertoire for understanding and solving difficult problems. Six capabilities you could build and combine.

Make policy work in the real world

Policy Engineering

How do we design policy that survives contact with engineers, users and actual organisational behavior?

Bring together domain expertise, behavioral insights, human-centered design and technology to create controls that people can understand, systems can implement and organisations can actually operate.

A technically correct policy that everyone works around is not a successful policy.

Turn uncertainty into decisions

Enterprise Risk Management

How do we help leaders decide which risks matter, what needs intervention and what we can deliberately live with? Connect signals across the organisation, expose dependencies and concentration risks, translate risk appetite into practical choices and bring better analysis to difficult decisions.

The output is not another register. It is a better decision.

Build assurance into the technology

GRC Platform Engineering

How do we make governance and assurance part of the delivery environment rather than another checkpoint around it? Build Policy-as-Code, automated evidence, continuous control verification and other infrastructure that makes safer behavior easier and assurance more timely.

Sometimes the answer is automation. Sometimes the smarter answer is removing the process first.

Govern systems that increasingly act for themselves

AI & Agentic Governance

What can an AI agent decide? Where must humans intervene? How should decision boundaries, accountability and assurance work when autonomous systems act at scale?

How do we govern model drift, changing behavior and GRC's own use of AI? Some answers exist. Many do not. You could help develop them.

Find the signal before it becomes the incident

Threat-Informed Risk Intelligence

How do we understand what is changing now rather than explain months later what went wrong? Connect cyber, data, resilience, platform, supply-chain and operational signals to identify patterns and emerging risks earlier.

Less: “Did the control pass?” More: “Is it working now, what changed, and what does that tell us?”

See the system everyone else sees in pieces

GRC Systems Architecture

How do policy, risk, controls, evidence, engineering and assurance fit together?

Design the taxonomies, information flows, feedback loops and operating models that allow them to work as one system. Ask some people about one control and they will explain the other three things it affects.

We like those people.

[What we are looking for]

Break the Frame

We are not looking for people to make yesterday's processes 10% faster. We want people willing to ask:

  • Why does this exist?

  • What risk are we actually managing?

  • What evidence says it works?

  • What behavior are we creating?

  • Could technology remove this step?

  • Could we design the problem away?

Sometimes the answer is better policy. Sometimes automation. Sometimes a different operating model. Occasionally, the right answer is to stop doing something altogether.

The expectation is not to challenge everything. It is to know what deserves to be challenged, why, and what should replace it.

What working here may feel like:

  • You will not always inherit a neatly defined problem.

  • Evidence may be incomplete. People may disagree about what is wrong.

  • A process may have existed so long that nobody quite remembers why.

  • Sometimes the problem you were asked to solve will turn out not to be the real problem.

That is part of the work.

Investigate before recommending. Prototype before standardising. Sit with engineers and users before writing policy. Use evidence before forming conclusions. Connect signals that others have not put together. And be willing to change your mind when your first hypothesis is wrong. We consider that progress.

What good looks like

Success is not the number of policies, findings, reports or dashboards produced. We are making progress when:

  • important risks are seen earlier

  • leaders make difficult decisions with better evidence

  • teams encounter fewer unnecessary governance touchpoints

  • policy is easier to understand, implement and verify

  • more assurance comes from live evidence

  • recurring problems are solved at system level

  • safer behavior happens increasingly by design

  • government can adopt AI and emerging technologies with greater confidence

  • governance helps delivery move faster rather than becoming the reason it slows down

And ultimately: Government uses technology better, essential services remain dependable, and citizens experience better public services without sacrificing trust. That is the measure that matters.

Who might find this interesting

There is no single background we are looking for.

You may come from engineering, cybersecurity, risk, assurance, resilience, AI, architecture, digital policy, product delivery, behavioural science, service design, design research, or somewhere less obvious.

Depth matters. But so does what happens when you reach the edge of what you know.

  • Do you get curious?

  • Can you make sense of messy information?

  • Can you work with people who see the problem differently?

  • Can you connect technical, organisational and human factors?

  • Can you turn an idea into something testable?

  • And when something clearly could work better, do you find it difficult to simply walk past?

For some of the problems we are tackling, the answer does not exist yet. That is precisely what makes them worth working on.

This may not be for everyone

If you are looking for a mature playbook, tightly defined boundaries and a portfolio that mainly needs maintaining, there are probably better roles. This work involves ambiguity, experimentation, difficult trade-offs and the occasional failed idea. But if a stubborn problem bothers you enough that you want to understand it, challenge assumptions and build something better, we should probably have a conversation.

Why GovTech

GovTech is in an unusual position. We help shape government technology policy. We build and operate major digital platforms. We can engineer governance and assurance into real delivery environments. We can test ideas against real-world problems and see whether they actually work. And what works here can become capability that benefits the wider Singapore Government.

So, this is not simply a chance to practice GRC differently. It is a chance to help discover what modern governance, risk and assurance needs to become.

What difficult problem would you like to help us solve?

Hosting Support Services provides coordinated operational and commercial support across government hosting environments, improving cost transparency, service quality, vendor management and agency choice.

The Programme must provide dependable foundations for critical services while simplifying cloud adoption, reducing fragmented operating practices and raising engineering standards across agencies.

The Programme is also shaping the next generation of AI-ready, sovereign and resilient infrastructure for government. Government Commercial Cloud (GCC) is a key platform within Singapore Government Technology Stacks that enables government agencies to build and operate digital services on commercial cloud. The GCC Engineering team develops platform automations, landing zones, and security tooling across AWS, Azure, and GCP — serving thousands of government systems and thousands of public officers.

Security at GCC is not a side function — it's core to the platform's value proposition. Government agencies trust GCC to be secure by default.

You are the single named owner of security outcomes across all engineering teams in GCC. You define how security works — the standards, processes, escalation paths, and technical approaches — and drive adoption through influence, not authority. You operate through a Security Champions network: persistent, named engineers in each product team who own security judgment locally, coordinated by you. Your accountability is whether GCC is actually secure — measured through process health, incident response quality, and security posture metrics you define.

This role is part of the organisation's domain leadership structure — you join alongside Engineering Managers as a peer, not as a report to any EM. The Security domain is being stood up fresh. The previous model (centralised security team gatekeeping all decisions) has been retired. You inherit a Champions network in early stages, documented runbooks, and interim coverage from a senior security advisor. Your job is to take it from "interim bridge" to "sustainable, scalable security function."

The domain scope will evolve. Today it centres on the areas listed above — but we expect the role to grow into adjacent areas (AI security, detection engineering) as the organisation's needs develop. Adaptability and willingness to define your own frontier matters more than deep expertise in every area on day one.

[What you will be working on]

Security Architecture & Posture

  • Own the organisation's security posture across all product teams and cloud environments
  • Architect security frameworks that integrate into engineering workflows without creating bottlenecks
  • Design and evolve threat modelling methodologies adapted to the organisation's multi-cloud, multi-tenant context
  • Define escalation paths, severity frameworks, and incident response playbooks
  • Own the relationship with GCSOC, shaping how external security signals translate into internal action
  • Drive security tooling strategy — selecting, configuring, and setting alert thresholds that distinguish signal from noise

Standards & Process Design

  • Define security standards, runbooks, and compliance approaches that teams can self-serve against
  • Design the Security Champions model: training curriculum, forum cadence, escalation criteria, and what "good" looks like for a champion
  • Replace gatekeeping with enablement — move from "security reviews everything" to "teams self-certify against clear criteria, you spot-check and consult"
  • Own security decision records: all posture choices documented, auditable, and transferable
  • Reform compliance processes (e.g. IMR8) to reduce ceremony while maintaining assurance

Cross-Org Influence

  • Drive security adoption across 5-6 engineering teams through the Champions network
  • Run a regular cross-org security forum: shared learning, emerging threats, pattern reviews
  • Consult on high-risk designs and architectural trade-offs when teams escalate
  • Handle genuine security incidents personally, with Champions as informed participants
  • Build security judgment across the engineering organisation — not by centralising decisions, but by raising the floor
  • Serve as the organisation's authoritative security voice on technical matters — advising on vendor evaluations, platform-level policy design, and cross-programme security decisions that require deep domain expertise beyond any single team's scope

Technical Depth

  • Maintain hands-on capability in at least two of: cloud security architecture, application security, supply chain security, detection engineering
  • Evaluate and prototype security tooling; make build-vs-buy recommendations grounded in the org's actual threat model
  • Contribute to or lead security incident post-mortems with root cause analysis that drives systemic improvement
  • Stay current on emerging threats and translate external signals into organisational action

[What we are looking for]

Must-Have

  • Deep security engineering expertise (architecture, not just operations) — you've designed security frameworks, not just followed them
  • Demonstrated ability to influence without authority across multiple engineering teams
  • Experience designing security processes that scale through enablement rather than gatekeeping
  • Strong enough as an engineer to review designs, read code, and earn credibility with senior SWEs
  • Clear, structured communication — you'll write strategies, runbooks, and decision records that outlive you
  • Comfort operating with ambiguity: this role is being stood up for the first time, and you'll shape what it becomes
  • Proficiency in scripting (Python, Bash) and working with APIs — you'll build and review automation, not just specify it
  • Solid understanding of identity, networking, logging, monitoring, and data security in cloud environments

Strong Signals

  • Experience with cloud security across multiple CSPs — ideally hands-on with native security services, not just console-level familiarity
  • Background in both offensive (threat modelling, VAPT, red team) and defensive (SIEM, detection engineering, incident response) security
  • Track record of building security champion or embedded security programs
  • Experience with CNAPP/CSPM platforms and vulnerability management tooling
  • Experience integrating security controls into CI/CD pipelines and DevSecOps workflows
  • Familiarity with compliance and threat frameworks and the judgment to know when compliance ≠ security
  • Experience working in government or highly regulated environments
  • Awareness of AI security risks and emerging governance frameworks

Technology Landscape

You'll encounter the following in this role. We don't expect mastery of all of these on day one — what matters is the ability to learn quickly and form sound judgment across unfamiliar tools.

| Area | Technologies |

|------|-------------|

| Cloud providers | AWS, Azure, GCP (multi-account/subscription/project at scale) |

| Security posture | Wiz, AWS Security Hub, Azure Defender, GCP Security Command Center |

| Vulnerability management | Nessus, Trivy, AWS Inspector, container scanning |

| SIEM & detection | Elastic SIEM, GuardDuty, Sentinel, CloudTrail/Activity Log |

| Identity & access | IAM (all CSPs), Entra ID, workload identity, RBAC/ABAC patterns |

| IaC & pipelines | Terraform, GitLab CI/CD, policy-as-code (OPA, Sentinel) |

| Secrets & supply chain | Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, SBOM tooling, dependency scanning |

| Compliance frameworks | IMR8, CIS Benchmarks, NIST CSF, ISO 27001, MITRE ATT&CK |

| Scripting & automation | Python, Bash, REST APIs |

| Emerging | AI/LLM security (OWASP LLM Top 10, NIST AI RMF), detection-as-code |

Preferred Certifications

Not required, but signal depth in relevant areas:

  • Cloud security: AWS Security Specialty, Azure Security Engineer Associate, GCP Professional Cloud Security Engineer
  • Security generalist: CISSP, CCSP, or relevant GIAC certifications
  • Offensive: OSCP, GPEN, or equivalent hands-on security testing credentials

Dealbreakers

  • Pure compliance/audit background with no engineering depth — this role requires technical credibility with senior engineers
  • Preference for centralised control ("everything goes through security") — the operating model is distributed enablement
  • Inability to document and codify decisions — if you leave, someone else must be able to pick up without an information gap

As a Lead Product Manager, you will shape the strategy and roadmap of the fCMS. This role is not about managing a fixed set of requirements. It is about helping the Judiciary modernise critical systems in a way that delivers value incrementally, reduces delivery risk and creates long-term adaptability. You will help the platform respond to new legislation, policies and judicial processes, while improving the experience of those who use and operate the courts.

Shape the future of justice in Singapore

Justice is one of Singapore's most important public services. Every year, almost 200,000 cases pass through our courts, involving individuals, families, businesses, lawyers and public agencies. Behind every case is someone seeking a fair, timely and accessible resolution.

The Judiciary's transformation into One Judiciary brought together the Supreme Court, State Courts and Family Justice Courts under a shared vision of delivering justice that is trusted, accessible and ready for the future.

Realising this vision requires more than organisational change. It requires rethinking the digital systems, processes and services that underpin how justice is delivered.

The Future Courts Management System (fCMS) is the Judiciary's flagship digital transformation programme, developed in close partnership with GovTech. You will join GovTech's product management community while working deeply with the Judiciary to shape products that support the administration of justice across Singapore's Courts.

This is not simply a like-for-like replacement of legacy systems. It is an opportunity to reimagine how court services should work: making them easier to use, more responsive to changing legislation and policies, and better able to serve everyone who depends on them.

This is a rare opportunity to help shape how justice will be delivered in Singapore for years to come.

In this role, you will:

  • Shape product strategy for fCMS domains, translating Judiciary priorities, user needs, operational complexity and legislative changes into clear roadmaps and measurable outcomes.

  • Work in a product trio with Engineering and Design leads to discover, prioritise and deliver solutions that are valuable, usable, feasible, secure and scalable.

  • Understand users and court operations by working with judges, judicial officers, lawyers, court administrators, partner agencies and members of the public to identify where digital products can make the greatest difference.

  • Deliver value incrementally using modern product and engineering practices that reduce delivery risk, support learning from real usage and avoid big-bang replacement.

  • Shape a secure and adaptable platform that can support evolving court processes, new government policies, integrations, data needs and long-term operational resilience.

  • Build alignment and product capability by communicating product direction clearly, influencing through evidence, and coaching or guiding Product Managers where appropriate.

  • You bring clarity to ambiguity — framing complex user, operational, legal and policy problems into clear product opportunities.

  • You think strategically and systemically — understanding how court processes, technology, legislation, data and organisational change connect across One Judiciary.

  • You make thoughtful product trade-offs — balancing user value, operational needs, technical sustainability, security, compliance and delivery risk.

  • You lead through influence — building alignment across senior stakeholders, court operations, legal, policy, design, engineering and technology partners.

  • You are comfortable with modern digital delivery — working with multidisciplinary teams, Agile delivery, cloud platforms, APIs, integrations, enterprise systems, product analytics and secure-by-design practices.

  • You raise the bar for product practice — coaching Product Managers where appropriate, contributing to GovTech's product community and strengthening a culture of discovery, evidence and continuous improvement.

Experience leading complex digital products, platforms or enterprise workflows is important. Experience in government, justice, regulated environments or large-scale transformation programmes will be advantageous, but not essential.

What Success Looks Like

In this role, you will help the Judiciary:

  • Improve access to justice by shaping digital services that are easier to use, more inclusive and better aligned to the needs of court users.

  • Modernise critical court operations by streamlining workflows across courts, case types and user groups.

  • Respond faster to change by enabling new legislation, policies and judicial processes to be implemented more quickly and consistently.

Few product management roles offer the opportunity to redesign digital systems that underpin an entire national institution.

The role blends deep, hands-on product ownership with leadership of a small and growing team of product managers, working day-to-day alongside agency stakeholders, policy owners, and design and engineering teams.

What you will be working on

Lead Product Manager — Access to Justice & Regulation, Ministry of Law (MLAW)

As Lead Product Manager for Access to Justice and Regulation at the Ministry of Law (MinLaw), you will lead the product strategy and transformation of two of MinLaw's major business verticals.

Your portfolio will span four product domains:

Assess to Justice

  • Legal — helping people who need legal assistance obtain and navigate representation.
  • Community — helping people resolve disputes early and turn legal outcomes into real-world resolution and compliance.

Regulation

  • Licensing — enabling legitimate operators to receive timely permission to operate without compromising regulatory safeguards.
  • Enforcement — helping regulatory teams detect and address risks before they cause serious harm.

Together, these products touch important moments for individuals, businesses and professionals — from seeking legal help and resolving disputes to entering and operating within regulated sectors.

You will help MinLaw rethink how these services should work, organise technology around enduring user problems and policy outcomes, and build the product teams and common capabilities required to deliver them.

In This Role, You Will

  • Own the product strategy across two domains: Access to Justice and Regulation, translating MinLaw's policy outcomes, user needs, operational challenges and technology opportunities into a coherent portfolio direction.
  • Lead and coach Product Managers, giving teams sufficient autonomy to solve their respective problems while ensuring that product strategies reinforce the outcomes of the wider vertical.
  • Define and use outcome measures, establishing meaningful measures of product success and using evidence to understand whether interventions are improving outcomes rather than simply delivering features.
  • Drive the transition from projects to products, establishing enduring ownership and continuous discovery and development instead of treating digitalisation primarily as a sequence of fixed-scope system implementations.
  • Partner deeply with policy and operations, understanding the intent behind legislation, regulation and government programmes while challenging historical processes that unnecessarily constrain user experience or operational effectiveness.
  • Work in close partnership with Engineering and Design leadership, ensuring that product strategy is desirable for users, feasible to build, operationally viable and technically sustainable.
  • Navigate complex product trade-offs, balancing accessibility, regulatory safeguards, policy intent, operational realities, security, cost, delivery risk and long-term sustainability.

You'll Thrive in This Role If...

  • You can lead at multiple levels of abstraction. You are comfortable moving from a conversation about MinLaw's strategic outcomes to a product strategy, an investment decision or a specific user problem — without losing sight of how they connect.
  • You think in portfolios, not just products. You understand that good product leadership sometimes means investing in one product, sharing capabilities across several, consolidating existing solutions or deciding not to build something at all.
  • You are an experienced product leader. You have led complex digital products or platforms and can coach Product Managers rather than needing to personally make every product decision.
  • You bring clarity to ambiguity. You can take complex policy, operational and user problems and turn them into clear product choices that multidisciplinary teams can act on.
  • You think in outcomes rather than systems. You naturally ask what problem we are solving and how we will know whether people's lives or regulatory outcomes have improved, rather than starting with a system, feature or predetermined solution.

Experience in government, legal services, regulation or similarly complex domains is advantageous, but not essential. We value demonstrated product leadership, judgement and the ability to learn complex domains over familiarity with a particular industry.

What Success Looks Like

You will have succeeded when:

  • MinLaw is managing Access to Justice and Regulation as products, not collections of systems and projects. Teams have clear ownership of enduring problems and outcomes, with strategies that persist beyond individual initiatives or technology refreshes.
  • There is evidence that the products are making a difference. Teams have meaningful measures of success and can demonstrate how their work is improving outcomes for the people, businesses and officers who rely on MinLaw's services.
  • MinLaw makes better portfolio choices. Investment decisions are increasingly driven by user and policy outcomes, evidence and strategic priorities — including deliberate decisions about what to build, reuse, consolidate, change or stop.
  • The portfolio becomes simpler over time. Common needs across products and regulatory regimes are solved through shared capabilities and platforms where appropriate, reducing unnecessary duplication and fragmentation.
  • Product teams can respond more quickly to change. New policies and emerging needs can increasingly be addressed by evolving existing products and capabilities rather than starting new technology projects from scratch.

Why This Role Is Different

This role sits at an unusual intersection of product leadership, law, regulation, public policy and technology.

You will not be responsible for a single application or transformation programme.

You will lead product strategy across two major areas of MinLaw's mission and work with multiple Product Managers and multidisciplinary teams to transform how those outcomes are delivered.

Some of the problems will require excellent individual products. Others will require common platforms or capabilities spanning several products. Some may be solved through data or AI. And sometimes the right product decision will be to simplify a process or change an operating model rather than build more technology.

The challenge is to see these connections and make deliberate choices about where product teams and technology can create the greatest public value.

The product portfolio, teams and practices you establish will shape how MinLaw delivers access to justice and regulation for years to come.

TradeNet is Singapore’s National Single Window for trade permit processing. It processes over 9 million permit applications annually across import, export and transshipment. We operate with high autonomy. Engineers are expected to think deeply, exercise sound judgement, and take ownership of technical decisions. You own the code from technical design through to production. We practice and value honest feedback, practical decision-making and real impact.

We are replacing the decades-old legacy system with a modern, cloud-native platform.The rebuild touches everything: decomposing a monolithic Java/J2EE application into cloud-native services, reconstructing undocumented business logic from incomplete legacy code, clearing compliance and data-governance constraints, and delivering a platform that multiple government agencies depend on daily.

The Chief Architect owns the technical coherence of this effort. You define how the system is structured, how teams interface with each other, and where the hard boundaries are. You work across product squads, TechOps, and programme leadership — but your authority is technical, not managerial.

About the role

You will build agentic offensive security tools: AI agents that find, validate and exploit vulnerabilities in applications, source code, cloud environments and infrastructure, the way a skilled red teamer would.
You are first and foremost a strong software engineer. You also know how attackers work, well enough to teach an agent to think like one. And you have built agentic applications before, so you know what it takes to make them reliable in production.
This is an applied AI role. You will build on top of large language models, not train them.

What you will do

  • Design and build production agentic systems that carry out security testing autonomously, covering planning, tool use, memory and multi-agent orchestration.

  • Turn attacker tradecraft into agent capability: translate attack techniques into tools, prompts, workflows and decision logic.

  • Build the tooling agents rely on, such as exploit harnesses, sandboxed execution environments, browser and API automation, and code analysis.

  • Build evaluation harnesses and benchmarks that measure how well agents find real vulnerabilities, how many false positives they raise, and what each run costs.

  • Reproduce and triage what the agents report, then feed the lessons back into the system.

  • Build in the controls that keep agents safe to run: target scoping, guardrails, human approval points and audit logging.

  • Ship and operate the software end to end: services, APIs, user interfaces, CI/CD, tests and observability.

  • Use AI coding assistants and agents in your own daily work, and raise the team's practice in doing so.

  • Lead technical design, review code and mentor other engineers.

  • Keep current with new attack techniques and with developments in LLMs and agent tooling.

Software engineering

The Singapore Judiciary plays a fundamental role in upholding the rule of law and ensuring that justice is accessible, effective and trusted.

For many people, navigating the justice system can be unfamiliar and complex. They may be representing themselves, dealing with a difficult personal situation, or interacting with the Courts for the first time. For lawyers, judicial officers and court staff, complex processes and systems can create a different set of challenges that affect how efficiently and effectively justice is delivered.

As the Senior Designer, you will help make the justice system easier to understand, navigate and participate in — while respecting the legal and procedural safeguards that underpin it.

You will work across the Judiciary with judges, judicial officers, court staff, lawyers, members of the public, self-represented persons, policy and technology teams to understand where people encounter barriers and design better ways for them to interact with the justice system.

This is not simply a role designing digital products. You will help shape how the Judiciary administers, adjudicates and delivers justice, using design, technology and service thinking to improve outcomes for both the people who use the system and the people who operate it.

The Opportunity

The opportunity is to make the justice system easier to understand, navigate and participate in — for the people who use it and the professionals who help deliver it.

This includes members of the public and self-represented persons who may have little or no experience with the Courts, as well as lawyers, paralegals, judges, judicial officers, court administrators and other agencies that interact with the justice system.

For users, accessibility can mean being able to find the right information, understand what they need to do, complete processes with greater confidence, and know what to expect next. For those delivering justice, it can mean having systems and processes that reduce unnecessary administrative burden and allow them to focus on the work that matters.

The challenge is not simply to make every process simpler. Some complexity is necessary because of legal, procedural and institutional requirements. The opportunity for design is to distinguish necessary complexity from accidental complexity — removing avoidable barriers while preserving the safeguards and integrity of the justice system.

Technology, digital services and the systems that support the Judiciary are important enablers of this transformation. By improving how information, processes and services work together, they can help the Judiciary respond more effectively to changing needs, procedures and legislation.

Ultimately, the goal is not the technology itself. The goal is a justice system that works better for the people who depend on it.

What you would do

Understand people and the system

You will research how people and professionals experience the justice system, identifying barriers, pain points and opportunities across services, processes and organisational boundaries. You will use research, workshops and prototyping to turn complex problems into clear opportunities and practical solutions.

Shape better ways of delivering justice

You will work with judicial, legal, policy, operational and technology stakeholders to shape how justice services should work in the future. You will identify whether problems are best addressed through technology, service or process redesign, information, policy or a combination of these. You will design systems and services that help the Judiciary administer, adjudicate and deliver justice more effectively, while making the experience easier to understand and navigate.

Bring people together

You will facilitate co-design and working sessions with judicial, legal, operational, technology and user groups to build alignment around better solutions. You will challenge assumptions constructively, communicate design decisions using research, data, prototypes and user perspectives, and create shared artefacts that help teams work from a common understanding.

Raise the bar for design

You will enforce design standards, patterns and practices that enable consistent, accessible experiences across Judiciary services. You will coach and mentor designers while improving how the team researches, designs, critiques and communicates its work. You will champion responsible use of AI and emerging tools to accelerate design while maintaining quality, accuracy and human judgement.

  • Strong portfolio demonstrating research, synthesis, interaction design, prototyping and delivery.

  • Experience designing complex workflows, professional users or high-stakes environments.

  • Strong systems-thinking ability and experience connecting user needs with organisational, operational and technology considerations.

Stakeholder leadership

  • Proven ability to facilitate alignment across groups with competing priorities and deeply held views.

  • Experience working with senior stakeholders and domain experts who are not design-literate.

  • Comfortable challenging assumptions and presenting design decisions with clarity and conviction.

  • Skilled at translating research and user needs into compelling narratives without oversimplifying complex issues.

  • Able to build trust and lead through influence rather than authority.

  • You are kind, direct and courageous in equal measure — willing to surface difficult problems while bringing people with you towards a better solution.

Ways of working

  • You think in systems but move quickly when the opportunity calls for it.

  • You maintain clear and accessible design artefacts so teams and stakeholders can work from a shared understanding of the current state.

  • Experience working in or with the Singapore public sector.

What You'll Do

  • Define and own what good data provisioning looks like across WOG — spanning Data Quality, Data Delivery Performance and Data Interfacing Standards — and iterate those standards in close collaboration with policy stakeholders, ensuring they remain grounded in what agencies can realistically implement as the ecosystem matures.

[About the role]

This is not a conventional procurement vacancy. It is an opportunity to build the operating models, capabilities and reusable knowledge that will shape how Procurement works across GovTech and, where useful, the wider Singapore Government.

What procurement problem won’t leave you alone?
Why does Procurement sometimes enter the conversation after the most important decisions have already been made?

Why do experienced procurement officers repeatedly solve similar problems, but the knowledge remains with individuals rather than becoming organisational capability?

Why do we improve individual steps in a process when the better question may be whether the process, control or operating model should exist in its current form at all?

As technology, markets and business models change, how should Procurement itself change?

If questions like these make you want to get underneath the problem, challenge the assumptions behind it and build something better, you should apply.

The Policy, Risk, Engagement and Competency (PREC) team in GovTech Procurement and Contracts Division (PCD) is rethinking how Procurement can work across GovTech and, where useful, the wider Singapore Government (ICT focused).

Why this matters
Procurement is more than getting a purchase through a process.

Done well, it helps teams make better decisions about what to buy, how to approach the market, how to structure commercial relationships and how to get better outcomes from suppliers.

At GovTech, we want simple and routine buying to become increasingly intuitive and self-service, while bringing Procurement in earlier where the problem is complex, strategic or commercially significant. At the Whole-of-Government level, we are exploring how ICT procurement capability, specialist expertise, commercial intelligence and learning can be better connected and reused.

That means PREC cannot just improve today’s processes. We need to help rethink how procurement should operate tomorrow.

The capabilities you could build and combine
You may begin with depth in one or two areas and develop a broader combination over time. The capabilities you draw on will depend on the problem.

Rethink how Procurement works
Procurement Operating Model & Transformation
How should Procurement organise itself as business and technology needs evolve? Explore what should be centralised, decentralised or delivered differently. Look across people, process, policy, data and technology rather than optimising each in isolation.

Get Procurement into the right conversations
Business Partnering
How can Procurement contribute before requirements and commercial approaches have already been decided? Build approaches that help Procurement engage earlier on complex decisions, understand business problems and bring commercial thinking to the table.

Turn individual expertise into organisational capability
Knowledge Productisation
How do we stop solving the same problem from scratch? Take knowledge that sits with experienced practitioners and turn it into reusable frameworks, tools, decision support and scalable assets.

Redesign, not just streamline
Process & System Redesign
Instead of asking, “How can we make this step faster?”, ask, “Why does this step exist?” Look end-to-end at how Procurement works and determine whether processes and controls should be eliminated, simplified, standardised, automated or redesigned.

Turn information into better decisions
Procurement Intelligence
Bring together procurement, supplier, pricing, market and organisational information so decisions are based on better evidence, not simply precedent. Identify patterns, opportunities and risks, and translate them into actionable recommendations.

Make good ideas travel
Whole-of-Government Capability & Learning
How can something that works in one team or agency become useful elsewhere? Identify effective approaches, codify the learning and help create procurement capabilities that can be reused across GovTech and potentially across government.

[What we looking for]
We are not looking for someone simply to make today’s procurement processes a little faster.

We want someone willing to ask:

  • What problem are we actually trying to solve?
  • Why does this process or control exist?
  • Does it still address the risk it was designed for?
  • Are we solving the same problem repeatedly?
  • Could the business make this decision itself with the right guardrails?
  • Could data or technology change how the work is done?
  • Should Procurement be involved earlier, later, differently, or sometimes not at all?
  • If we redesigned this from scratch today, would we build it this way?

Sometimes the answer will be a better process. Sometimes it will be a different operating model, clearer decision rights, better information or a reusable capability. Occasionally, the answer may be to stop doing something.

The expectation is not to challenge everything. It is to understand what deserves to be challenged, why, and what should replace it.

[What good looks like]
Success is not the number of policies, templates, papers or improvement initiatives produced.

We are making progress when:

  • Procurement gets involved at the point where it can genuinely influence an outcome.
  • Simple buying becomes simpler.
  • Complex procurement decisions benefit from stronger commercial thinking.
  • Teams spend less effort repeatedly solving problems that have already been solved.
  • Procurement knowledge becomes reusable organisational capability rather than remaining with individuals.
  • Processes and controls are designed around the problems and risks they are actually meant to address.
  • Good practices can be adapted and reused beyond the team that developed them.
  • Procurement becomes a function that business teams seek out for the value it brings, not simply because a process requires them to engage us.

We are looking for a Product Manager to explore and build high-value use cases for AI context layers across government.

AI systems are only as reliable as their understanding of the underlying data. The same term or data field may have different meanings or calculation logic across different government agencies. Without that context, people and AI tools misinterpret data, give wrong answers, or fail to combine sources.

Context layers capture that missing meaning by organising the definitions, business rules, relationships and provenance around government data, in a form both people and AI systems can use.

In this role, you would:
1. Agency context layers — help government agencies identify use cases where context matters most, pilot and build their own context layers, and ensure these can be easily maintained and repeatable across other agencies.
2. A cross-agency context layer — work out how shared meaning can be established across agencies, so data and AI applications work across domain boundaries.

This is an early-stage, zero-to-one product role. You will work closely with agencies, policy owners, data teams, engineers, and users to test hypotheses, deliver practical prototypes, and determine which capabilities should be scaled as common government products or standards.

[What you will be working on]

As a Product Manager, you will hold significant ownership over your product domain, driving it from concept to reality while aligning with the broader programme goals. Your core responsibilities include:

Set the product strategy

  • Define the vision for government context layers and the use cases they should enable.

  • Translate an ambiguous problem space into testable product hypotheses, priority user journeys, and a sequenced roadmap.

  • Define the relationship between agency-specific context layers and shared cross-agency capabilities.

  • Decide what GovTech should build centrally, offer as reusable components, set as standards, or leave to agencies.

  • Align product, engineering, data, AI, policy and agency leadership.

Help agencies build their own context layers

  • Build a network of partner agencies willing to co-develop and test use cases

  • Lead discovery into agencies' data, terminology, business rules, user needs and existing knowledge assets

  • Prioritise high-value operational, analytical, service-delivery and AI use cases, and define success measures for each

  • Ground every context layer in a real product or workflow, not a documentation exercise

  • Define how context layers connect to data platforms, AI systems, search tools, analytics environments and digital services, while meeting security, performance and data governance standards.

  • Test operating models, from agency-led to centrally supported to shared services, and identify adoption barriers such as unclear ownership, maintenance effort and skills gaps.

  • Turn lessons from pilots into reusable playbooks, patterns, tools and onboarding.


Build a cross-agency context layer

  • Identify use cases that need concepts, entities and relationships understood across agency boundaries.

  • Explore how differing definitions, taxonomies, identifiers and data models can be mapped or reconciled.

  • Build and validate prototypes that combine context from multiple agencies for discovery, decision support, analytics or AI applications.

  • Agree ownership, stewardship, contribution and maintenance models for shared context.

  • Work with agencies on trust, provenance, access controls and accountability.

Measure and iterate

  • Define and track product metrics that show real value (e.g. AI answer accuracy, time saved, reuse of context) rather than vanity metrics.

  • Run structured experiments and user studies to validate product decisions and prioritise the roadmap.

  • Maintain a clear, well-reasoned product backlog and communicate trade-offs transparently to stakeholders.

  • At least 5 years of relevant experience, including 3 or more in product management within cross-functional teams of engineers, designers and data or platform specialists

  • Strong product sense and product management experience — including ability to do zero-to-one product discovery experience in ambiguous problem spaces

  • Experience delivering data or AI products, with a working understanding of data governance, provenance, access control and information security

  • Comfort working with engineers on APIs, data models, integration patterns, retrieval systems and AI-enabled applications

  • Strong facilitation and stakeholder management across organisations with different incentives, without direct authority over them

  • Strong analytical skills — comfortable using data to diagnose problems, validate hypotheses, and communicate product performance

  • Prior experience with knowledge graphs, ontologies, taxonomies, metadata standards or semantic modelling

  • Experience designing federated operating models: knowing when to set common standards versus localised mappings

  • Experience in or with government agencies, or other large federated organisations where adoption depends on coordination rather than top-down mandate

  • Background in building or evaluating retrieval-augmented or agentic AI systems

  • Diploma/Degree in Computer Science, Infocomm Technology, Engineering, or a related subject area, or prior working experience in product management, IT business analysis, application solutioning design and testing.

  • Experience in modern product development and management practices such as Agile, Design Thinking, and Product-Centric Development will be strongly preferred.

[About Giant Robots Labs]

Giant Robots Labs is the experimental technology lab inside GovTech's Government Technology Office. We turn ambitious ideas into working products quickly, test them with real users, and operate the promising ones through prototype and limited beta. We also experiment with the lab itself: how small teams are organised, how software gets built when agents do much of the work, and what a product operation needs to look like when a pilot can reach real users in weeks.

Product operations usually exists because coordination, documentation and reporting are expensive manual work. Much of that work is now automatable, and we would rather automate it than staff it. So this is not a role that administers a process, maintains a backlog on someone else's behalf, or turns status into slides. It is the role that makes the lab run: deciding which problems become pilots, clearing the unglamorous path that stands between a working prototype and a real government user, and making sure we can tell whether any of it worked.

[What you will be working on]

  • Run pilot intake. Help decide which problems become pilots, what question each pilot is actually testing, and when it has been answered.
  • Clear the path to real users. Data sharing, security and classification review, agency sponsorship, accounts and access: a pilot team should spend its weeks building, not waiting.
  • Own the operational side of limited beta, including user onboarding and support, incident response, cost and quality monitoring, and the dull reliability work that decides whether an agency trusts us with the next thing.
  • Instrument pilots so that continue-or-kill decisions rest on usage and evidence rather than on who argues hardest.
  • Keep the lab's context legible. Decisions, hypotheses, results and abandoned approaches, recorded in a form that both people and agents can read and act on.
  • Build the lab's internal tooling and automation, agentic where that is the right answer, for the coordination and reporting work that would otherwise eat a team's attention. Where you can build it yourself, build it.
  • Design the lab's ways of working, keep them light, and retire them when they stop earning their keep.
  • Hold the GovTech interfaces: platform teams, identity, data infrastructure, procurement, legal, security. Know who answers which question, and be owed enough favours that the answer arrives in a day.
  • Prepare successful pilots for what comes next, with the evidence, runbook, cost picture and open risks that a productisation team needs in order to pick one up.
  • Notice when a pilot is drifting. No users, an untestable hypothesis, a prototype quietly becoming a system somebody has to run forever. Raise it early, including when nobody wants to hear it.
  • Run the lab's own measurement. How fast pilots move, how many reach real users, what they cost to operate, and which of our decisions turned out to be wrong.
  • Help new people and new teams get productive, which in a lab like this means tools and context more than induction decks.
  • Experiment with the organisation itself. Team shapes, role boundaries, where agents sit in a team, and an honest read on whether last quarter's experiment worked.
You will thrive here if
  • You would rather build or automate an operation than administer one, and you reach for a script, a workflow or an agent before a recurring meeting.
  • You are comfortable that the process does not exist yet and that part of your job is deciding how little of it we need.
  • You enjoy the unglamorous blockers. Approvals, access, classification, procurement and support are where pilots quietly die, and you find it satisfying to kill those delays permanently rather than route around them each time.
  • You can hold an opinion about whether a product is working, and defend it with evidence in a room full of people who built it.
  • You are willing to say that a pilot should stop.
  • You work comfortably with engineers and designers as a peer rather than as coordination between them.
  • You are hands-on with AI tools and curious about what they make unnecessary, including parts of your own job.
  • You are energised by lean teams, broad ownership and problems that change shape every few months.

[What we are looking for]

  • Around 5 to 8 years in product operations, programme or product management, business operations, delivery or a similar role, in an environment where software actually shipped.
  • Evidence you have built or materially changed how a team works, rather than maintained how it already worked. We will ask what you introduced, what you removed, and how you knew which was which.
  • Comfort with data. You can get to the numbers yourself, through SQL, spreadsheets, a BI tool or an analytics stack, and you know the difference between a metric that drives a decision and one that decorates a report.
  • Technical fluency sufficient to work closely with engineers: you can read a system diagram, follow a deployment, understand what an API or an integration implies, and automate your own work.
  • Practical fluency with AI tools, including agentic ones such as Claude Code, Codex or equivalents, and interest in using them to replace operational toil.
  • Clear writing. Much of this role is making a decision, a risk or a result legible to people who were not in the room.
  • A track record of high agency: things that happened because you decided they should.
Public sector experience, zero-to-one product environments, or having been the first operations hire somewhere are all strong pluses. None is required.

What you can expect
  • A role defined by what the lab needs rather than by a fixed set of artefacts to produce.
  • Direct access to users, agency partners, stakeholders and decision-makers, with no brief passed down a chain.
  • Real influence over which pilots start, continue and stop.
  • Freedom to automate your own work, and to argue that a practice is not worth keeping.
  • A wide variety of problems and domains across the Singapore public sector.
  • A lab that is willing to change how it organises itself based on evidence, including evidence that you gather.
  • Colleagues who own products end to end, and who will expect the same standard of ownership from you.

[What you will be working on]

The AI Programme builds shared AI infrastructure that agencies can run in production, instead of rebuilding the same foundations independently. It sits within Government Digital Products, and it owns a small number of central products that a lot of other people's work now depends on.

Three of them shape the job. There's the agent surface public officers use to get through the day: it reaches into their mail, their documents and their case systems, so it has to be quick, honest about what it just did on their behalf, and safe to point at real records. Underneath sits the developer platform, where teams across government bring their own agents, MCP servers and skills and move them into production through review, approval and audit. And there's the model and capability layer that most agencies meet first: a compliant gateway to multiple production-approved models behind an OpenAI-compatible API, alongside shared speech, vision and document capabilities (live transcription, image and video classification, key information extraction) that every agency would otherwise go and procure separately, with guardrails, quotas and cost attribution already attached.

Building an agent demo is easy now, and that's fine, because it means the hard parts have moved. Most of what we work on lives after the demo. An agent decides to call a tool that sends an email on someone's behalf, and the approval gate for that has to be enforced by the runtime, not requested politely in a system prompt. A tool loop needs a stop condition that doesn't depend on the model deciding it's done. Token spend has to trace back to the team that caused it, and when an agency's agent gets slower this week, someone has to be able to say why. Rollback gets interesting when the artefact is a prompt, a tool schema and a model version rather than a binary. Very little of that is model work. It's orchestration, platform and operations, which is roughly the job.
You'll work across all of it: the surfaces officers see, the runtime underneath, the platform other engineers build on, and the unglamorous business of keeping the whole thing up. Your user is a public officer with something to finish today. Your customer is often another engineering team in another agency.

What you'll do

  • Build and run the surfaces officers use daily. Streaming, approval interrupts, resumable sessions, and interfaces that stay readable when an agent is doing four things at once

  • Build the runtime beneath them: tool orchestration, approval gates enforced in code, loop limits, per-turn tool filtering, memory and checkpointing, model routing and fallback

  • Work on the platform half, where the job is to let other teams onboard their own agents, MCP servers, skills and models, with the policy checks and promotion workflows that let them move to production safely and repeatedly

  • Extend the shared capability APIs (speech, vision, document extraction) and keep them fast and cheap enough that agencies reach for them instead of building their own

  • Integrate with what government already runs: identity, mail and calendar, document stores, agency line-of-business systems, the existing CI/CD pipelines

  • Instrument the things you'll want to argue about later. Tool call traces, latency, error taxonomies, cost per team and per feature

  • Build evaluation into delivery, so changing a prompt, a tool or a model becomes a measurable decision instead of an argument

  • Run it. Deployments, incidents, capacity, cost, and the support queue of officers who found the case nobody thought of

  • Work with agency teams as users and as builders, and turn the third bespoke request into a platform feature

  • Take part in security and privacy reviews on the assumption that these systems get audited, because they do

You'll thrive here if

  • You want the thing you wrote to be used by someone doing real work the next morning

  • You're interested in what happens after launch, not only up to it

  • The constraints (classification, audit trails, approvals, cost accountability) read to you as design problems rather than obstacles to route around

  • You have a view on what belongs in a prompt and what belongs in the backend, and you'll defend it

  • You'd rather ship something narrow and run it properly than demo something broad

  • You use agentic coding tools every day and have opinions about where they help and where they quietly cost you

  • You can talk to a policy officer in the morning and debug a streaming protocol after lunch

  • You expect the model layer to change under you every few months, and you design so that's survivable

[What we are looking for]

We're deliberately open on background. This is a broad role, and the strongest signal is something you built, shipped and then had to keep running, not a number of years.

Your primary focus is NAC's centralised data platform, an integrated environment that consolidates fragmented arts datasets from across the sector. The platform equips NAC and partner agencies with tools to track participation, monitor funding outcomes, and make evidence-based decisions on resource allocation and policy development.

This is a cross-sector product serving both internal NAC officers and external partner agencies, across varying levels of data literacy and distinct workflows. You will gather design requirements together with product managers, engineers, and NAC stakeholders, translating data and policy needs into clear, testable design direction.

As the first designer on the ground, you will also help establish design practice within NAC ITD and shape what comes next as the portfolio grows.

Design Data-Dense Experiences

Design dashboards, visualisations, and analytical interfaces that make complex datasets legible and actionable across a diverse user base. Apply deliberate information architecture and cognitive load management, not just visual design.

Gather and Translate Requirements

Work with product managers, engineers, and stakeholders across NAC and partner agencies to surface the actual need behind a stated request. Translate data and policy requirements into clear, testable design briefs.

Own the Full Design Lifecycle

Take features from concept to production: user flows, wireframes, high-fidelity UI, prototypes, and engineering handoff. Move efficiently across the full stack of UX without needing to be managed through each stage.

Conduct Continuous Research

Run focused usability tests and user interviews to validate how different user groups interpret and act on data. Synthesise findings quickly and feed them back into the design without waiting for a formal research cycle.

Manage Stakeholders Across Agencies

Navigate a complex stakeholder environment across NAC divisions and partner agencies. Communicate design rationale clearly and build trust with stakeholders who may not have worked with a designer before.

Contribute to the Design System

Extend shared CCYC design system components and patterns to cover data visualisation and dashboard use cases. Document contributions clearly for the wider design team

  • Experience: 7+ years of UX or product design experience, with a portfolio that includes at least one shipped data product: dashboards, analytics tools, or reporting interfaces.

  • Data UX: Demonstrable experience designing data visualisations and dashboards: chart selection, information hierarchy, filtering patterns, and handling of empty, partial, and error states.

  • Requirements Gathering: Experience gathering requirements for data or analytics products, working with PMs and engineers to translate domain needs into design direction.

  • Autonomy: Ability to set your own priorities and operate independently without close supervision.

  • Tools: Proficiency in Figma for UI design, prototyping, and design system contribution.

  • Prior experience in a government digital environment or statutory board context.

  • Experience contributing to a component-based design system at scale.

Pioneer role with genuine end-to-end ownership, working on a technically complex problem that directly shapes how Singapore's arts sector is understood and funded.
